title: Using `move_to` on a numpy array with negative stride crashes the Python process
body:
The `move_to` function we have for moving arrays from one namespace to another can crash the Python process when you ask it to move an array with negative strides. I found this while working on `PCA` where we have an array with negative stride (`Vt` from `_fit_truncated`).

The code below is a reproducer:

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
import sklearn
from sklearn.utils._array_api import get_namespace_and_device, move_to

def make_negative_strided():
    """A small, contiguous-source array viewed with a negative stride."""
    a = np.arange(12.0).reshape(3, 4)[:, ::-1]
    assert not a.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"]
    assert a.strides[-1] < 0
    return a

a = make_negative_strided()
with sklearn.config_context(array_api_dispatch=True):
    xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(torch.asarray([1.0]))
    try:
        move_to(a, xp=xp, device=device)
    except Exception as exc:  # it is not caught
        print("Caught a Python exception (unexpected):", type(exc).__name__, exc)
    else:
        # this doesn't happen
        print("move_to returned without error (unexpected)")

    # instead the process exits with a SIGABRT
```

AI tells me that a possible fix is to call `np.ascontiguousarray(array)` if the input `array` is an array with negative stride. In addition we should [only apply this workaround in the case where the `move_to` target is torch](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34307#issuecomment-4778962780). The comment for the workaround should also include a link to https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/188023 and this issue so we can know when the work around can be removed.

Something like this, but with a check for torch as target:
```diff
--- a/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
+++ b/sklearn/utils/_array_api.py
@@ def move_to(*arrays, xp, device):
             xp_array, _, device_array = get_namespace_and_device(array)
             if xp == xp_array and device == device_array:
                 converted_arrays.append(array)
             else:
+                strides = getattr(array, "strides", None)
+                if strides is not None and any(
+                    stride < 0 for stride in strides
+                ):
+                    # Some libraries (e.g. torch) do not raise a catchable
+                    # Python exception but abort the whole process when a NumPy
+                    # array with negative or zero strides is imported via DLPack
+                    # (such arrays are produced for instance by ``a[::-1]``
+                    # reversals, as done by ARPACK). The ``except`` clause below
+                    # therefore cannot protect against it, so the source array is
+                    # made contiguous first to guarantee positive strides.
+                    array = numpy.ascontiguousarray(array)
                 try:
                     # The dlpack protocol is the future proof and library agnostic
                     # method to transfer arrays across namespace and device boundaries
                     # hence this method is attempted first and going through NumPy is
                     # only used as fallback in case of failure.
                     # Note: copy=None is the default since array-api 2023.12. Namespace
                     # libraries should only trigger a copy automatically if needed.
                     array_converted = xp.from_dlpack(array, device=device)
```

What do others think about this? I am also wondering if this is a bug in numpy's DLPack implementation (should not expose arrays with negative stride) or if this is a bug in torch (should check for negative stride before doing anything)?

I think that `numpy.ascontiguousarray(array)` is free for most arrays, those that already full fill it. For arrays that are not already contiguous I don't know what the cost is, but I think there is no alternative?

title: `CalibratedClassifierCV(method="sigmoid")` should always take the raw logits as inputs instead of the predicted probabilities
body: This is a defect [I first observed while reviewing the temperature scaling PR](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31068#discussion_r2012459507): if the uncalibrated classifier only exposes a `decision_function` and no `predict_proba` (which is the case for SVMs for instance) our implementation of sigmoid calibration (aka Platt-scaling) is fine because the output values of `decision_function` are morally logits between -inf and +inf with 0 as the default decision threshold. But if the uncalibrated classifier already exposes a `predict_proba` method (e.g. `GaussianNB`), our current implementation takes the predicted probabilities as input of the parametrized sigmoid function. This is incorrect: we should the log of the probabilistic predictions (incremented by a small epsilon) to feed logits as inputs to the sigmoid function. I had started an unfinished WIP branch now turned into a draft PR (https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34313) to attempt to fix this problem and started to do empirical evaluation to assess the impact of this change in examples. Early results were very promising. However, it would now need work to be sync with main again after the merge of the temperature scaling PR and I got distracted and this was burried in my personal TODO list of WIP stuff to revive. Meanwhile, the following paper by @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller et al. was published, and it confirms that it is empirically much better to take the logits, in which case it is a very competitive calibration method (better than most other calibration methods on average on a large set of data & model pairs). CalArena: A Large-Scale Post-Hoc Calibration Benchmark https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30188 Side note: I suspect that OvR Platt-logits followed by post-hoc class-wise renormalization would also work very well in the multiclass setting, but this does not seem to have been explored in the above paper from a cursory glance. Do you confirm @eugeneberta, @dholzmueller?

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When `radius` is passed as a per-sample array, `NearestNeighbors.radius_neighbors` returns a correct result with `n_jobs=1` but raises a `ValueError` with `n_jobs>1` on identical input for both `ball_tree` and `kd_tree`. An `n_jobs` value should not change behavior.

`NearestNeighbors` is a convenient interface to `BallTree` and `KDTree` because, unlike those, it accepts an `n_jobs` parameter.

I used the following workaround in the past, [here](https://github.com/nicolassalvy/ClippedDensityCoverage/blob/main/ClippedDensityCoverage/metrics/Clipped_Density_Coverage.py#L52-71):
```python
tree = NearestNeighbors(
    algorithm="ball_tree", n_jobs=n_jobs
).fit(data1)

distances, indices = (
    tree.radius_neighbors(
        X=data2,
        radius=np.max(radii),
        return_distance=True,
        sort_results=False,
    )
)

correct_indices = [
    indices[i][distances[i] <= radii[i]]
    for i in range(len(distances))
]
```
but this can be very slow, both because of the mandatory `return_distance=True` and because of the following: adaptive radius search is useful here because the typical distances in different data modes can be very different, one mode where they are very far apart and another where they are close. title: Reconsider zero-affinity row fallback in LabelPropagation/LabelSpreading (fit + predict_proba) to mathematically valid probability distributions
body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Right now, when a row has zero affinity to any labeled data (e.g., an isolated training point in `fit`, or a faraway query point in `predict_proba` via #34350), both code paths use the same fallback:

`normalizer[normalizer == 0] = 1`

This prevents a `0/0` `NaN` crash, but it results in a row of all zeros (e.g., `[0.0, 0.0]`).

This breaks the strict mathematical docs of `predict_proba`, which requires returning a valid categorical distribution where the row sums to 1.0. This issue is to standardize a mathematically valid fallback so downstream metrics don't silently choke on malformed probabilities.

### Describe your proposed solution

Replace the `[0.0, 0.0]` fallback with a shared internal helper function that applies a mathematically valid distribution across both `fit` and `predict_proba`.

**Options for the fallback:**
1. A uniform distribution (`1/n_classes` per class) -> Honestly represents "no info".
2. The training set's empirical class priors.
3. Keep `[0, 0]` but emit an explicit `UserWarning` so pipelines can catch the degenerate case.

**Why this matters for downstream consumers:**
I tested the practical impact of the current `[0, 0]` fallback on common metrics:
- `log_loss`: Throws a `UserWarning` but still calculates a heavily distorted score. In my test, a single zero-row inflated the loss from 0.23 to 12.17.
- `roc_auc_score`: Silently swallows the array and treats `[0, 0]` as a confident negative prediction (the exact opposite of "no information").
- `predict()`: Silently `argmax`es the all-zero row to class 0.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

1. **Leave it as-is:** The current `normalizer == 0 -> 1` fix was added in #19271 as a pragmatic stopgap to fix a hard crash (#9292). It solved the crash, but left the math broken. Extending this same stopgap to `predict_proba` (#34350) just doubles down on the technical debt.
2. **Fix only `predict_proba`:** We could leave `fit()` alone to preserve backward compatibility for `label_distributions_` and only fix the public-facing `predict_proba`. Ideally, both should share the same semantics, but fixing `predict_proba` is the higher priority since it pipes directly into user metrics.

### Additional context

- #9292 — Original `NaN` crash report.
- #19271 — The PR that introduced the `normalizer == 0 -> 1` stopgap in `fit`.
- #34350 — Current PR extending the stopgap to `predict_proba`.

*Note:* This isn't about reverting the crash fix from #19271 (which was necessary), but rather upgrading the fallback value from a math-breaking `[0, 0]` to a valid probability distribution.

title: Separate control over response surfaces and class boundaries in `DecisionBoundaryDisplay`
body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Originally posted in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/33108#issuecomment-4861934626.

Currently, `DecisionBoundaryDisplay.from_estimator` does not allow users to control whether decision boundaries are drawn or to customize their line style. Although users can customize the surface through `**kwargs`, passing parameters such as `linewidth` or `color` to style the boundary may instead affect the surface and lead to unexpected behavior.

### Describe your proposed solution

I have a suggestion regarding the `DecisionBoundaryDisplay.from_estimator` API. I propose the following interface:

```python
@classmethod
def from_estimator(
    cls,
    estimator,
    X,
    *,
    grid_resolution=100,
    eps=1.0,
    plot_method="contourf",
    response_method="auto",
    class_of_interest=None,
    target_colors=None,
    show_class_boundaries=False,  # new
    response_kwargs=None,         # new
    boundary_kwargs=None,         # new
    xlabel=None,
    ylabel=None,
    ax=None,
):
```

```text
show_class_boundaries : bool, default=False
    Whether to overlay boundaries between predicted classes.

    The boundaries are computed from discrete predictions and are independent
    of the main response displayed by `plot_method`.

response_kwargs : dict, default=None
    Additional keyword arguments passed to the plotting call for the main
    response, such as `alpha`, `levels`, or `zorder`.

boundary_kwargs : dict, default=None
    Additional keyword arguments passed when drawing class boundaries, such as
    `colors`, `linewidths`, `linestyles`, or `zorder`.
```

This API would provide separate and more explicit control over the response surface and the class boundaries, including their colors and other plotting properties.

One open question remains: when `plot_method="contour"` and `response_method="predict"`, `show_class_boundaries` would effectively need to be `True`; otherwise, there would be nothing to display. Perhaps `show_class_boundaries` should instead accept `"auto"`?

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

The PyPI wheel bundles `libgomp.so.1.0.0-8.5.0-28.el8_10.alma.1.x86_64.debug` which is probably not what we want.

Despite scikit-learn [building in manylinux_2_28](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b2958e8ac0da5f56fe82677c2a67ed960f8d3a89/.github/workflows/wheels.yml#L100), whose [docs say](https://github.com/pypa/manylinux#manylinux_2_28-almalinux-8-based) the toolchain is GCC 14, the bundled OpenMP runtime is effectively AlmaLinux 8 / GCC 8.5-era libgomp.

Codex suggests to add this repair command around [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/b2958e8ac0da5f56fe82677c2a67ed960f8d3a89/.github/workflows/wheels.yml#L194) to the linux build:

            LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/rh/gcc-toolset-14/root/usr/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
            auditwheel repair -w {dest_dir} {wheel}
```

`auditwheel repair` decides which concrete shared object to copy into `scikit_learn.libs` (what is bundled in the PyPi wheel). Without help, it resolves the base AlmaLinux 8 runtime. With `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` pointing to gcc-toolset first, it should resolve to the newer gcc-toolset libgomp.

title: AdaBoostClassifier/Regressor.feature_importances_ has dead error-handling code
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Found this while poking around `_weight_boosting.py`. feature_importances_ has this check at the top:

```python
if self.estimators_ is None or len(self.estimators_) == 0:
    raise ValueError("Estimator not fitted, call `fit` before `feature_importances_`.")
```

estimators_ doesn't exist until you fit the model, so accessing it before fit fails with a plain AttributeError before the code even gets to check "is it None". And after fitting, estimators_ is never empty either.

So that whole ValueError branch is just dead code, nobody's ever going to hit it. Other ensembles like RandomForestClassifier handle this with check_is_fitted(self), which gives a proper NotFittedError instead. Seems worth swapping this to match.

Also noticed while I was in there: there's a separate except AttributeError branch a few lines down for when the base estimator doesn't have feature_importances_ at all (e.g. LogisticRegression). That one's real and reachable, but there's no test for it currently.

from sklearn.ensemble import AdaBoostClassifier
AdaBoostClassifier().feature_importances_
```

### Expected Results

Should raise a proper NotFittedError (using check_is_fitted(self), like other ensemble methods do), instead of failing with a raw AttributeError.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Found this while poking around _gb.py. _resize_state has a check meant to give a clear error if you try to shrink n_estimators:

```python
if total_n_estimators < self.estimators_.shape[0]:
    raise ValueError(
        "resize with smaller n_estimators %d < %d"
        % (total_n_estimators, self.estimators_[0])
    )
```

self.estimators_[0] is wrong there, it grabs an actual fitted estimator object instead of self.estimators_.shape[0] (the count). Since %d can't print a non-number like that, it crashes with a confusing TypeError instead of giving the intended clean error.

You'd never actually see this through normal fit() calls though, since fit() already checks the same thing earlier and raises its own ValueError first, so _resize_state's version never gets a chance to run. That's also why the existing test for this still passes, it's checking the earlier error, not this one, so the bug's been sitting here unnoticed.

from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier

gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=5)
gb.estimators_ = np.empty((10, 1), dtype=object)
gb._resize_state()

title: PowerTransformer raises raw TypeError on Pandas nullable integer (Int64) and float (Float64) dtypes containing pd.NA
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

When passing a Pandas `DataFrame` containing modern nullable extension dtypes (such as `Int64` or `Float64`) with missing values (`pd.NA`) into `PowerTransformer`, the estimator crashes with an unhandled internal exception (`TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`) rather than coercing the array cleanly or raising a standard scikit-learn `ValueError`.

### Context & User-Facing Impact

1. **Modern Pandas Integration:** With modern Pandas workflows (including Pandas 2.0+ defaults and `df.convert_dtypes()`), nullable integer and float types are standard when working with tabular data that contains missing values.
2. **Pipeline Failures:** In production data pipelines, passing a DataFrame with nullable dtypes directly into a scikit-learn `Pipeline([('power_transform', PowerTransformer()), ...])` causes the entire pipeline to fail with a low-level Pandas boolean evaluation error instead of processing the data smoothly.
3. **Unnecessary Workarounds:** To bypass this bug, users currently have to manually write boilerplate pre-casting logic (e.g., `df.astype("float64")`) before calling `PowerTransformer`, which breaks scikit-learn's native DataFrame compatibility goals.
4. **Consistency:** Most scikit-learn estimators handle Pandas extension arrays seamlessly by converting them to standard floating-point NumPy arrays via `_validate_data`. `PowerTransformer` should follow this same pattern.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer

# Minimal DataFrame using Pandas nullable integer extension dtype ('Int64')
# The missing value (None) is automatically represented as pd.NA
X = pd.DataFrame({"col": pd.Series([1, 2, None, 4], dtype="Int64")})

# Triggers raw TypeError inside PowerTransformer during internal array checks
pt = PowerTransformer(method="box-cox")
pt.fit_transform(X)
```

### Expected Results

`PowerTransformer` should automatically coerce Pandas nullable extension arrays into standard IEEE floating-point NumPy arrays (`np.float64` or `np.float32`) via `_validate_data` before evaluating numerical bound checks.

Specifically:
- It should not crash with a raw `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous`.
- Passing data with nullable dtypes should either complete successfully (coercing `pd.NA` to `np.nan`) or raise a clear, standardized `ValueError` if input constraints are violated.

### Actual Results

The estimator crashes with a raw `TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous` during internal positivity checks (`X <= 0`):

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "reproduce_bug.py", line 9, in <module>
    pt.fit_transform(X)
  File "sklearn/base.py", line 1478, in fit_transform
    return self.fit(X, **fit_params).transform(X)
  File "sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py", line 3218, in fit
    return self._fit(X, y, force_transform=False)
  File "sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py", line 3232, in _fit
    if np.any(X <= 0):
  File "pandas/core/ops/common.py", line 81, in new_method
    return method(self, other)
TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.3
executable: /usr/bin/python3
   machine: Linux-6.8.0-generic-x86_64

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.0
       pandas: 3.0.4
   matplotlib: 3.9.0
       joblib: 1.4.2
threadpoolctl: 3.5.0
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I am interested in opening a Pull Request to fix this issue once it has been triaged!

### Root Cause Analysis

In `PowerTransformer._fit` (inside `sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py`), positivity and finite bounds checks—such as `np.any(X <= 0)`—are executed on the input `X` **before** array validation occurs:

```python
# Current order of execution in _fit():
if np.any(X <= 0):  # <--- Fails here on Pandas ExtensionArrays containing pd.NA
    raise ValueError(...)

X = self._validate_data(X, ...)

title: explained_variance_score returns a perfect 1.0 for a single sample (silently breaks LeaveOneOut CV)
body:
### Describe the bug

`explained_variance_score` returns `1.0` (a perfect score) for a single sample no
matter how wrong the prediction is, and emits no warning. `r2_score`, its
documented sibling, guards the same degenerate case with an
`UndefinedMetricWarning` and returns `nan`.

With one sample there is no variance to explain, so the numerator
(`Var(y_true - y_pred)`) and the denominator (`Var(y_true)`) are both `0`, and
`force_finite` maps `0/0` to `1.0` — documented as "perfect predictions" — even
when the prediction is plainly wrong.

The practical consequence is that **`LeaveOneOut` cross-validation scored with
`explained_variance` silently reports a perfect 1.0 for any model, including one
fit on pure noise.**

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import explained_variance_score, r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut, cross_val_score

# 1) single sample, clearly wrong prediction
print(explained_variance_score([1.0], [2.0]))  # 1.0, no warning
print(r2_score([1.0], [2.0]))                  # nan + UndefinedMetricWarning

# 2) the practical impact: LeaveOneOut on pure noise
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X, y = rng.normal(size=(12, 3)), rng.normal(size=12)

ev = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=LeaveOneOut(),
                     scoring="explained_variance")
r2 = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=LeaveOneOut(), scoring="r2")
print(ev.mean())  # 1.0   <- perfect score on noise, silently
print(r2.mean())  # nan   <- correctly undefined
```

### Expected Results

Something that does not claim a perfect fit on a single sample. Matching
`r2_score` seems most consistent: emit `UndefinedMetricWarning` and return `nan`
when `n_samples < 2`, since the metric is not defined without variance to
explain.

### Actual Results

```
1.0        # explained_variance_score([1.0], [2.0]) -- no warning
nan        # r2_score([1.0], [2.0]) -- UndefinedMetricWarning

1.0        # LeaveOneOut + explained_variance on pure noise
nan        # LeaveOneOut + r2 on pure noise (12 UndefinedMetricWarnings)
```

### Versions

```
System:
    python: 3.14
Python dependencies:
    sklearn: 1.9.0
```

### Notes

I appreciate that ignoring a systematic offset is intentional for this metric
(the docstring notes it), so the `n_samples >= 2` behaviour is not in question
here — only the single-sample case, where there is no variance at all and the
score is silently reported as perfect.

I'm happy to open a PR adding the same `n_samples < 2` guard that `r2_score`
already uses, if that's the direction you'd prefer.

title: `UnionFind.fast_find`'s path compression never touches the queried node — quadratic linkage labelling
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`UnionFind.fast_find`'s path-compression loop never actually shortens the path of the node it was called on, so path compression is effectively disabled. `fast_find` degenerates to a plain, uncompressed find. Callers that build a dendrogram (e.g. `make_single_linkage`) allocate a new parent node per merge, so single-linkage/chaining inputs produce O(n)-deep union-find trees; with compression disabled, the repeated uncompressed finds sum to **O(n²)**. This is invisible on small inputs but dominates end-to-end runtime at scale (tens of seconds at n≈200k in a comparable reproduction — see the linked hdbscan report for measured numbers against the same code pattern).

**File:** `sklearn/cluster/_hierarchical_fast.pyx` — `UnionFind.fast_find`
**Also affects:** `sklearn/cluster/_hdbscan/_linkage.pyx::make_single_linkage`, which calls `UnionFind.fast_find` in its inner loop; and, within `sklearn/cluster/_agglomerative.py`, `AgglomerativeClustering(linkage="single")` / `FeatureAgglomeration(linkage="single")`, both of which route through `_hierarchical.single_linkage_label` / `_hierarchical._single_linkage_label` (the unconstrained and connectivity-constrained paths, respectively) in `linkage_tree()`. Other linkages (`ward`, `average`, `complete`) use a separate heap + `IntFloatDict` implementation and are **not** affected.
**Type:** performance (results are correct; time is quadratic)
**Related:** the same defect exists independently in the `hdbscan` package (`scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan`, `hdbscan/_hdbscan_linkage.pyx`), which has its own vendored copy of this `UnionFind`. Bug report: [https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan/issues/731](https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan/issues/731).
**LLM usage**: found using Claude, reviewed manually.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np, time
from sklearn.cluster._hierarchical_fast import single_linkage_label

def build_L(K):
    rows = []
    w = 0
    for i in range(K - 1):
        rows.append((i, i + 1, w)); w += 1
    for i in range(K):
        rows.append((i, K + i, w)); w += 1
    return np.array(rows, dtype=np.float64)

prev_t = None
for K in [1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000]:
    L = build_L(K)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    single_linkage_label(L)
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    dt = t1 - t0
    ratio = dt / prev_t if prev_t else None
    print(f'K={K:6d}  n_samples={2*K:6d}  time={dt:.4f}s  ratio={ratio}')
    prev_t = dt
```

### Expected Results

Each doubling increases the runtime by a factor close to 2.

### Actual Results

```

K=  2000  n_samples=  4000  time=0.0068s  ratio=3.608907289229676

```

### Interest in fixing the bug

## The code

```cython
# sklearn/cluster/_hierarchical_fast.pyx
cdef class UnionFind(object):

    def __init__(self, N):
        self.parent = np.full(2 * N - 1, -1., dtype=np.intp, order='C')
        self.next_label = N
        self.size = np.hstack((np.ones(N, dtype=np.intp),
                               np.zeros(N - 1, dtype=np.intp)))

    cdef void union(self, intp_t m, intp_t n) noexcept:
        self.parent[m] = self.next_label
        self.parent[n] = self.next_label
        self.size[self.next_label] = self.size[m] + self.size[n]
        self.next_label += 1
        return

    @cython.wraparound(True)
    cdef intp_t fast_find(self, intp_t n) noexcept:
        cdef intp_t p
        p = n
        # find the highest node in the linkage graph so far
        while self.parent[n] != -1:
            n = self.parent[n]
        # provide a shortcut up to the highest node
        while self.parent[p] != n:
            p, self.parent[p] = self.parent[p], n
        return n
```

## Root cause

The "shortcut" line

```cython
p, self.parent[p] = self.parent[p], n
```

is a chained tuple assignment `target1, target2 = rhs1, rhs2`. Cython (like Python) evaluates the full right-hand side first — as a tuple, using the *current* value of `p` — and only then performs the assignments, **left to
right**:

1. Evaluate `rhs = (self.parent[p], n)` using the old `p`.
2. Assign target 1: `p = rhs[0]` — `p` is rebound *now*, to its old parent.
3. Assign target 2: `self.parent[p] = rhs[1]` — but this indexes with the **already-updated** `p` from step 2, not the node the loop meant to compress. The write lands one hop up from where it was intended.

The node originally passed to `fast_find(n)` is therefore never repointed at the root; only its ancestors shift by one hop per call. Reproducing the assignment in isolation:

```python
>>> parent = [1, 2, 3, -1]          # chain 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3(root)
>>> p, n = 0, 3
>>> p, parent[p] = parent[p], n     # one iteration of the "compression" loop
>>> p, parent
(1, [1, 3, 3, -1])                  # node 0 STILL points at 1 — untouched
```

Every subsequent `fast_find(0)` re-walks `0 → 1 → 3`, and this compounds across the whole tree, producing the O(n²) behavior.

## Impact

- Any caller that builds a chained union-find structure and repeatedly calls `fast_find` on it is quadratic in the number of points, dominated by re-walked, uncompressed paths. This includes `make_single_linkage` in `sklearn/cluster/_hdbscan/_linkage.pyx` (used by HDBSCAN) and `AgglomerativeClustering(linkage="single")` /
  `FeatureAgglomeration(linkage="single")` in `sklearn/cluster/_agglomerative.py`.
- **Results are unaffected.** `fast_find` still returns the correct root (the outer `while self.parent[n] != -1` loop correctly finds it), so linkage/hierarchy output is unchanged; this is purely a performance bug.

## Suggested fix

Walk to the root first, then compress every node on the path in a second pass. This sidesteps the tuple-assignment aliasing trap entirely:

```cython
cdef intp_t fast_find(self, intp_t n) noexcept:
    cdef intp_t root, nxt
    root = n
    while self.parent[root] != -1:
        root = self.parent[root]
    while self.parent[n] != -1 and self.parent[n] != root:
        nxt = self.parent[n]
        self.parent[n] = root
        n = nxt
    return root
```

Roots are unchanged, so output is bit-identical; only the amortized complexity of repeated `fast_find` calls improves (from effectively uncompressed to near-inverse-Ackermann with compression restored).

## Notes

- See the companion `hdbscan` package report (linked at the top of this file) for a worked measurement of the same pattern in a near-identical (ndarray-backed, rather than memoryview-backed) `UnionFind`.

title: dump_svmlight_file segfaults with multilabel=True and a 1D target array
body:
### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`sklearn.datasets.dump_svmlight_file` terminates the Python interpreter with a segmentation fault when `multilabel=True` is combined with a one-dimensional target array.

The input passes the public API parameter validation because `y` is array-like and `multilabel` is a boolean. However, the implementation subsequently appears to treat each scalar `y[i]` as an iterable collection of labels.

The following closely related input combinations work correctly:

- A sequence of label sequences such as `[[0], [1]]` with `multilabel=True`.
- A one-dimensional target array with `multilabel=False`.

A one-dimensional `y` may be invalid when `multilabel=True`, but a public scikit-learn API should reject it with a clear `TypeError` or `ValueError`. It should never terminate the entire Python process.

This can crash notebooks, data-processing pipelines, services, or other applications that pass incorrectly structured target data to this function.

## Steps/Code to Reproduce

The following self-contained script runs the problematic public API call in a child process because the call terminates the interpreter:

```python
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

if len(sys.argv) > 1:
    import numpy as np
    from sklearn.datasets import dump_svmlight_file

    X = np.zeros((2, 2))
    y = np.array([0, 1])

    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".svm") as tmp:
        dump_svmlight_file(X, y, tmp.name, multilabel=True)

    raise SystemExit(0)

import sklearn

print("sklearn", sklearn.__version__)

result = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, __file__, "child"],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
)

status = (
    f"signal {-result.returncode}"
    if result.returncode < 0
    else f"exit {result.returncode}"
)
print(f"  child -> {status}")

if result.returncode < 0:
    print(
        "BUG REPRODUCES: dump_svmlight_file(multilabel=True, 1-D y) "
        "kills the interpreter instead of raising"
    )
    raise SystemExit(1)

print("OK: call raises or returns instead of crashing")
```

Run it with:

```shell
python sklearn-001.py
```

### Expected Results

The function should reject the incompatible combination of `multilabel=True` and a one-dimensional target array with a Python exception, such as a `TypeError` or `ValueError`.

For example:

```text
ValueError: When multilabel=True, y must be a sequence of label sequences.
```

The Python interpreter should remain alive.


### Actual Results

The child process is terminated by `SIGSEGV`:

```text

BUG REPRODUCES: dump_svmlight_file(multilabel=True, 1-D y) kills the interpreter instead of raising

title: PCA does not discard singular values equal to zero
body:

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

In PCA, if an input matrix has linear dependencies, some singular values will be zeros, which also makes the components in that case be zeros.

These have no effect on the results and should be omitted, since they effectively aren't components, just padding, but scikit-learn doesn't discard them.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)

n = 10
S = rng.standard_normal((n+1, n))
S = S.T@S
mu = rng.standard_normal(size=n)
X = rng.multivariate_normal(mu, S, size=100)
X[:, 2:5] = X[:, [0]]

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
pca = PCA().fit(X)

import polars as pl
pl.DataFrame(pca.components_)
```

### Expected Results

title: Zero `sample_weight` raises ValueError in IsolationForest and Bagging estimators when bootstrap=False
body:
### Describe the bug

Since 1.8.0, `_generate_bagging_indices` draws row indices with
`random_state.choice(..., replace=bootstrap_samples, p=normalized_sample_weight)`.
When `bootstrap=False`, numpy's `choice` requires **at least `max_samples` non-zero
entries in `p`**, so any `sample_weight` containing zeros raises

```
ValueError: Fewer non-zero entries in p than size
```

Zero-weighting a row is the documented way to exclude it from a fit, and it is what
`sample_weight=0` means everywhere else in the library, so this is ordinary input.

`IsolationForest` is affected **on its defaults** (`bootstrap=False`,
`max_samples="auto"` → `min(256, n_samples)`). The crash fires whenever
`np.count_nonzero(sample_weight) < min(256, n_samples)`, which for any dataset of
256 rows or fewer means **a single zero weight is enough**:

| `n_samples` | zero weights needed to crash |
|---|---|
| 80 | 1 |
| 256 | 1 |
| 300 | 45 |
| 1000 | 745 |

`BaggingClassifier` / `BaggingRegressor` with `bootstrap=False` are affected the same
way. They at least emit `UserWarning: When fitting ... with sample_weight it is
recommended to use bootstrap=True`; `IsolationForest` emits nothing before crashing.

This is a regression from #31414 (merged June 2025, first released in 1.8.0). The
behaviour is unchanged on `main`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest

X = np.random.RandomState(0).uniform(size=(80, 4))
w = np.ones(80)
w[0] = 0.0          # exclude exactly one row, the documented way

IsolationForest(random_state=0).fit(X, sample_weight=w)
```

### Expected Results

A fit equivalent to deleting the zero-weighted rows, which is what happens today if
you do the exclusion by hand:

```python
IsolationForest(random_state=0).fit(X[w > 0])   # works fine
```

### Actual Results

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py", line 143, in _generate_bagging_indices
    sample_indices = random_state.choice(
  File "numpy/random/mtrand.pyx", line 1032, in numpy.random.mtrand.RandomState.choice
ValueError: Fewer non-zero entries in p than size
```

### Suggested fix

Without replacement you can only draw rows that have non-zero weight, so clamp the
request to the available support. Zero-weighted rows are then excluded exactly as if
they had been deleted:

```diff
--- a/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py
+++ b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py
@@ -85,6 +85,10 @@ def _generate_bagging_indices(
         )
     else:
         normalized_sample_weight = sample_weight / np.sum(sample_weight)
+        if not bootstrap_samples:
+            # Sampling without replacement can only draw rows that have a
+            # non-zero weight, so requesting more than that is not satisfiable.
+            max_samples = min(max_samples, np.count_nonzero(sample_weight))
         sample_indices = random_state.choice(
             n_samples,
             max_samples,
```

Verified with this patch applied:

- the reproducer above and the `Bagging*` equivalents all fit;
- `sklearn/ensemble/tests/test_bagging.py` and `test_iforest.py` pass (160 passed);
- over 300 draws, zero-weighted rows are never selected, each draw yields exactly the
  70 available non-zero rows, and indices stay distinct;
- the `bootstrap=True` path is untouched and still samples proportionally to weight.

title: BUG: Callback's _worker_connections cache grows too big

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Using a `ScoringMonitor` in a lot of sub-estimators in sub-processes eventually raises an `EOFError` when trying to create the connection for the callback to communicate across processes.

After investigating with the help of an LLM, the suspect appears to be the `_worker_connections`. It stores new connections for each fit, but there is no mechanism to remove them from the cache. When persistent workers are used, like when using joblib's loky backend, the cache grows until the worker process hits its fd limit and the next time a connection is opened the handshake sequence breaks mid-flight, causing the EOFError.

The LLM's suggested fix is to have a max size for `_worker_connections`, using a least recently used eviction policy.

title: BUG sample-weight ignored by `min_sample_leaf` in HGBDT
body:
## Description

In the following [course](https://probabl-ai.github.io/calibration-cost-sensitive-learning/content/notebooks/prevalence_correction.html#solution), we are using the weight of HGBDT to correct probability estimate. We know that it should be equivalent with a post-hoc correction. However, they are not equivalent for HGBDT while it works for logistic regression. In the past, we thought that it was due to the binning but it has been fixed (cf. #29641).

## Potential cause (to be check further)

`Splitter` in `sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/splitting.pyx` applies `min_samples_leaf` to histogram **counts** (`n_samples_left` / `n_samples_right`), not to the sum of sample weights (or hessians). Loss gradients/hessians (and bin edges after #29641) are weighted correctly.

## Minimal reproducer

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=1000,
    n_features=10,
    n_informative=5,
    n_redundant=0,
    weights=[0.75, 0.25],
    random_state=0,
)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
sw = rng.randint(1, 4, size=len(y))
X_rep, y_rep = np.repeat(X, sw, axis=0), np.repeat(y, sw)


def max_raw_diff(min_samples_leaf):
    est = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
        min_samples_leaf=min_samples_leaf,
        early_stopping=False,
        max_iter=50,
        random_state=0,
    )
    weighted = clone(est).fit(X, y, sample_weight=sw)
    repeated = clone(est).fit(X_rep, y_rep)
    return np.max(np.abs(weighted._raw_predict(X) - repeated._raw_predict(X)))


print(max_raw_diff(1))   # ~1e-8
print(max_raw_diff(20))  # ~2.4, unexpected
```

Observed on `main` (`1.10.dev0`):

- `min_samples_leaf=1`: max `|raw_pred|` diff ≈ `4.6e-08`
- `min_samples_leaf=20`: max `|raw_pred|` diff ≈ `2.42`

## Expected behavior

Expect equivalence.

## Notes

- Documented limitation in `test_sample_weight_effect` (forces `min_samples_leaf=1`).
- Related: #26128 (histogram counts vs weights). Not a regression of #29641; remaining gap after that fix.

### Introduce yourself

I am saikrishna working as a senior data engineer I have bachelors degree in computer science with data analytics specialization where I have worked on wide variety of tools like numpy, pandas, scikit-learn,... Where i have done various projects using various tools. Now I was reading the source looking for a bug to fix, part of it while testing a piece of code i have come across this. So i wanted to contribute and help tool perform better.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

so the `split_sign=True` makes `transform` return `2 * n_components` columns and the rest of the class does not know this. A `DictionaryLearning(split_sign=True)` step inside a `Pipeline` fits without any issue initially and then raises at `predict`.

so this has 3 symptoms:
- `get_feature_names_out()` returns half the names
- `set_output(transform="pandas")` raises `Length mismatch`
- float32 input comes back as float64

This also affects all three sparse-coding transformers: `DictionaryLearning`, `MiniBatchDictionaryLearning`, `SparseCoder`.

Previous works:
- #11000 already has DictionaryLearning and MiniBatchDictionaryLearning checked off as dtype-preserving.

- #32077 brought `SparseCoder` into the common tests and yet the float32 upcast survives in all the three because no common tests sets `split_sign=True`.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import DictionaryLearning
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(60, 5) + 0.5

print("float32 input -> output dtype:", dl.transform(X.astype(np.float32)).dtype)

pipe = make_pipeline(
    DictionaryLearning(n_components=4, split_sign=True, random_state=0), Ridge()
)
pipe.fit(X, y)
pipe.predict(X)

float32 input -> output dtype: float32

```python
expected_n_components = dictionary.shape[0]
if self.split_sign:
    expected_n_components += expected_n_components
```
It expects `2 * n_components` and undoes the split. But `_n_features_out` in the same
file returns the unsplit count in all three classes:
- `SparseCoder` line 1412
- `DictionaryLearning` line 1750
- `MiniBatchDictionaryLearning` line 2334

`test_dict_learning_split` in `sklearn/decomposition/tests/test_dict_learning.py`, and it
only exercises `transform` and `inverse_transform` and no common test sets `split_sign=True`.

fix can be, make `_n_features_out` account for `split_sign` in all three,
allocate the split array with the input dtype, and have `fit_transform` apply the same
split `transform` does.

The following scikit-learn test fails intermittently or consistently on i586 with Python 3.14.7:

```text
sklearn/callback/tests/test_callback_support.py::test_function_no_callback_support[RecordingCallback-processes-2]
```

The failure occurs only for the process-based case with `n_jobs=2`. The thread-based cases and the `n_jobs=1` case pass.

## Environment

- scikit-learn: 1.9.0
- Python: 3.14.7
- Architecture: i586
- joblib: 1.5.3
- pytest: 9.0.3
- pytest-xdist: 3.8.0
- OS: openSUSE Tumbleweed

## Reproduction

Run:

```bash
pytest -q sklearn/callback/tests/test_callback_support.py \
  -k 'test_function_no_callback_support'
```

The failing parameter combination is:

```text
test_function_no_callback_support[RecordingCallback-processes-2]
```

The relevant test code creates a callback-bearing estimator and sends it to process workers through joblib:

```python
callback = RecordingCallback()
estimator = MaxIterEstimator(max_iter=7).set_callbacks(callback)

Parallel(n_jobs=2, prefer="processes")(
    delayed(clone_and_fit)(estimator) for _ in range(5)
)
```

## Actual result

The test fails while joblib/cloudpickle serializes the task:

```text
RuntimeError: list changed size during iteration
when serializing dict item 'record'
when serializing sklearn.callback.tests._utils.RecordingCallback state
when serializing sklearn.callback.tests._utils.RecordingCallback object
```

This is then reported by joblib as:

```text
_pickle.PicklingError: Could not pickle the task to send it to the workers.
```

Full traceback excerpt:

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../joblib/externals/loky/backend/queues.py", line 159, in _feed
    obj_ = dumps(obj, reducers=reducers)
  ...
  File ".../joblib/externals/cloudpickle/cloudpickle.py", line 1313, in dump
    return super().dump(obj)
RuntimeError: list changed size during iteration

when serializing dict item 'record'
when serializing sklearn.callback.tests._utils.RecordingCallback state
when serializing sklearn.callback.tests._utils.RecordingCallback object
```

## Expected result

The test should complete successfully, as it does for:

```text
RecordingCallback-threads-1
RecordingCallback-threads-2
RecordingCallback-processes-1
RecordingAutoPropagatedCallback-processes-2
```

## Analysis

`RecordingCallback` stores its records in a regular list:

```python
self.record = []
self._listener_handle = open_listener(self.record.append, owner=self)
```

When the worker processes execute the estimator, callback messages are sent back to the parent process. The listener thread appends those messages to `callback.record`.

At the same time, joblib/cloudpickle serializes the estimator and callback to send work to another process. This means that cloudpickle can be iterating over `callback.record` while the listener thread appends to it.

The failure appears to be a timing-dependent race between callback message handling and process-task serialization. It was observed on i586, where the slower execution may make the race easier to trigger. I have not determined whether this is caused by a Python 3.14 behavior change, or whether Python 3.14 merely exposes an existing race in the test or callback implementation.

Could this test or callback state be made safe to pickle while callback records are being received? For example, should the live recording state be excluded from the pickled state, synchronized during serialization, or otherwise handled specially?

title: OneHotEncoder unknown-category warning is incorrect for columns without an infrequent category
body:
### Introduce yourself

I'm learning ML engineering and use scikit-learn for a delay-prediction model on
US flight data. This is the first issue I've opened. I encountered this while working out how to encode categorical columns that may contain previously unseen values during prediction.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

Carrier and destination can't be enumerated ahead of time, so both go to one
encoder with `drop="first"`, `handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"` and
`min_frequency=4`. On my first CV fold, 41,901 rows, it fits to:

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['HDN'], dtype=object)]
```

Destination gets an infrequent bucket. Carrier gets `None` because its rarest value has 148 rows in that fold and 744 across the training pool, so it is not below `min_frequency=4`. Transforming a row with an unknown carrier and an unknown destination produces this warning:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown
categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

The warning claims that the unknown categories in both columns will go to the infrequent category, but this is not true for the carrier feature because no `infrequent_sklearn` column exists for it, and the transformed row is zero across the entire carrier block.

This matters because `drop="first"` drops the encoded feature for the first carrier category (`AA` in this fold), making all zeros its carrier encoding. An unknown airline and a real flight belonging to `AA` therefore produce an identical carrier encoding, so the model treats them the same with respect to the carrier feature.

I caught this by inspecting `infrequent_categories_`, transforming a row containing an unknown carrier and destination, and comparing the resulting vector with `get_feature_names_out()`. The carrier block was entirely zero, even though the warning said that the unknown carrier would be encoded as the infrequent category. The warning should have identified that the unknown carrier was encoded as all zeros, while the unknown destination was routed to its infrequent bucket.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import warnings

from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

# Column 0: "a" and "b" both appear twice, so it has no infrequent category.
# Column 1: "y" appears once, so it does have an infrequent category.
X = [["a", "x"], ["a", "x"], ["b", "x"], ["b", "y"]]

encoder = OneHotEncoder(
    drop="first",
    sparse_output=False,
    handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist",
    min_frequency=2,
).fit(X)

print("infrequent_categories_:", encoder.infrequent_categories_)
print("feature names:         ", encoder.get_feature_names_out())

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    X_trans = encoder.transform([["c", "z"]])

print("transform([['c', 'z']]):", X_trans)
print("warning:", caught[0].message)
```

Both columns receive an unknown category, but only column 1 has an infrequent
category that can absorb it.


### Expected Results

The warning should describe what actually happens to each column. Column 1 has
an infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded there. Column 0 has
no infrequent category, so its unknown value is encoded as all zeros, which is the same encoding `drop="first"` assigns to the dropped category.

Something along the lines of:

```
Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. The unknown
categories in columns [1] will be encoded as the infrequent category. Those in
columns [0] will be encoded as all zeros, because these columns have no
infrequent category.
```

This is also what the `handle_unknown` docstring already documents:

> If the `'infrequent'` category does not exist, then `transform` and
> `inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
> `handle_unknown='ignore'`.


### Actual Results

```
infrequent_categories_: [None, array(['y'], dtype=object)]
feature names:          ['x0_b' 'x1_infrequent_sklearn']
transform([['c', 'z']]): [[0. 1.]]
warning: Found unknown categories in columns [0, 1] during transform. These unknown categories will be encoded as the infrequent category.
```

No exception is raised. The problem is that the warning talks about both columns and
makes a single claim about them, which is false for column 0: its
`infrequent_categories_` entry is `None`, no `x0_infrequent_sklearn` column
exists in `get_feature_names_out()`, and the transformed row is `0` across the
whole column-0 block.

Also reproduced on main (1.10.dev0) at a456b324bc, with identical output.

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.9 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Oct 21 2025, 19:11:29) [Clang 20.1.8 ]
   machine: macOS-26.5.2-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
          pip: 25.2
   setuptools: None
        numpy: 2.5.2
        scipy: 1.18.1
       Cython: None
       pandas: 3.0.5
   matplotlib: None
       joblib: 1.5.3
threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
     narwhals: 2.25.0

Built with OpenMP: True
```

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I would be interested in opening a PR if this is triaged as a bug.

The warning message is selected once from `handle_unknown`, but the actual outcome is determined separately for each column in `_map_infrequent_categories` (`sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py`). I would update the warning to distinguish columns that have an infrequent category from those that fall back to all zeros, update the affected warning assertions, and add a regression test for the mixed case above.

title: StratifiedGroupKFold returns an empty fold when n_groups == n_splits: least-populated-fold tiebreak is defeated by 1-ULP noise
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

### Describe the bug

`StratifiedGroupKFold` can return an empty test fold even when `n_groups >= n_splits`, because the "least populated fold" tiebreak in `_find_best_fold` is defeated by 1-ULP floating-point noise.

`_find_best_fold` selects a fold with:

```python
is_current_fold_better = fold_eval < min_eval or (
    np.isclose(fold_eval, min_eval)
    and samples_in_fold < min_samples_in_fold
)
```

The first branch uses an exact `<`. When two candidate folds are *mathematically* tied, `np.std` still returns values that differ by an ULP or two, so `fold_eval < min_eval` fires and that fold wins outright — the `samples_in_fold` comparison never runs. That comparison is the "heuristic for assigning group to the least populated fold in cases when all other criteria are equal" documented in the changelist comment at the top of `_iter_test_indices`, and in practice it is largely unreachable.

When `n_groups == n_splits` there is no slack: a single misdirected group leaves a fold with nothing in it.

This is distinct from #33085, which was about `n_groups < n_splits` and was addressed by #33176 (that PR was titled "Towards #33085" and the issue remains open).

**Impact.** `cross_val_score` silently produces `nan` for the empty fold, so the aggregate score becomes `nan`:

```python
scores: [0.6  0.375  nan  0.6]   ->  mean nan
```

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedGroupKFold

y = [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0, 2, 0, 2, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0]  # 3 classes, 6 samples each
g = [0, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 3, 3, 0, 2]  # 4 groups, sizes 5/3/2/8

for i, (tr, te) in enumerate(StratifiedGroupKFold(n_splits=4).split(y, y, g)):
    print(f"fold {i}: n_train={len(tr):2d} n_test={len(te):2d}")
```

### Expected Results

Four non-empty test folds. With 4 groups and 4 splits the assignment is forced to one group per fold.

```
fold 0: n_train=16 n_test= 2
fold 1: n_train=15 n_test= 3
fold 2: n_train=13 n_test= 5
fold 3: n_train=10 n_test= 8
```

### Actual Results

```
fold 0: n_train=13 n_test= 5
fold 1: n_train=10 n_test= 8
fold 2: n_train=18 n_test= 0    <-- empty test fold
fold 3: n_train=13 n_test= 5
```

`shuffle` does not help: all 24 relabellings of the four groups, and all of `random_state=0..199` with `shuffle=True`, still produce an empty fold.

### Mechanism

Instrumenting the assignment loop, the second group is the decisive one:

```
-- group 1 counts=[0, 1, 2]
     fold 0: eval=0.12028130608117205  samples_before=0
     fold 1: eval=0.12028130608117205  samples_before=0
     fold 2: eval=0.12028130608117205  samples_before=0
     fold 3: eval=0.12028130608117203  samples_before=2   <- 1 ULP lower
     -> chose fold 3
```

Three folds are empty, fold 3 already holds a group, and all four evaluations are mathematically identical. Fold 3 wins on a 1-ULP artefact, and fold 2 is never filled.

Measured over 15898 group-assignment decisions from randomised configurations:

- 7.0% of decisions have two or more mathematically tied folds whose winner is decided by floating-point noise (median deciding difference **1 ULP**, max 3).
- In 6.9% of all decisions the intended least-populated-fold tiebreak would have selected a *different* fold than the one actually chosen.

### Additional counterexamples

Found by random search; all reproduce identically on 1.9.0 and 1.10.dev0.

| `n_splits` | `n_groups` | `n` | fold sizes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 4 | 22 | `[6, 11, 0, 5]` |
| 6 | 6 | 24 | `[4, 6, 6, 0, 4, 4]` |
| 4 | 4 | 20 | `[4, 9, 0, 7]` |
| 5 | 5 | 13 | `[2, 3, 4, 0, 4]` |

Every failing case I found is at `n_groups == n_splits`; with one spare group I found none in ~25k configurations either way.

### Suggested fix

Require a strictly-better evaluation to be better by more than noise, so the tiebreak becomes reachable:

```python
is_tied = np.isclose(fold_eval, min_eval)
is_current_fold_better = (fold_eval < min_eval and not is_tied) or (
    is_tied and samples_in_fold < min_samples_in_fold
)
```

With that change the reproducer yields `[2, 3, 5, 8]`, and in a sweep of the sensitive regime (`n_splits` 2-6, `n_classes` 2-4, `n < 40`) empty folds go from **4/73401 to 0/73401**. `pytest --pyargs sklearn.model_selection` is unchanged at 642 passed / 238 skipped.

Two caveats worth discussing:

1. **It changes roughly 21% of splits.** That is the size of the latent defect rather than an over-aggressive tolerance: tightening `np.isclose` to `rtol=1e-9` or `1e-12` gives the same 21%, because these are true ties; exact equality drops churn to 0.3% but does not fix the bug.
2. **Stratification quality is essentially unchanged** — mean fold-size CV 0.2393 both ways, mean per-fold class-proportion deviation 0.10618 vs 0.10620 over 4000 configurations. This is a correctness fix for the degenerate case, not an improvement to stratification (cf. #24656).

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.13.9 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Oct 21 2025, 19:11:29) [Clang 20.1.8]
   machine: macOS-26.6-arm64-arm-64bit-Mach-O

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.10.dev0
        numpy: 2.6.0.dev0
        scipy: 2.0.0.dev0

threadpoolctl: 3.6.0

Also reproduced on released sklearn 1.9.0 with numpy 2.5.2 / scipy 1.18.1.
```

title: BUG: `QuantileTransformer()` sub-sampling impact is too high for sparse matrices
body: ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact Related to #34298 and #32585 For very sparse columns falling in the sub-sampling path, the number of actually sampled data will be `self.subsample * len(column_nnz_data) // n_samples`, which for the default `subsample=10_000` and 0.1% sparsity is 10... Which can quickly get noising. This can cause a lot of samples to collapse to 1 after fit-transform, distorting the output distribution weirdly. title: Investigation: Meson silently downgrades -O3 to -O2 under conda-forge CFLAGS
body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

Meson's `buildtype: release` implies `-O3` for every compiled extension in the project. Under conda-forge, it doesn't: conda-forge's compiler activation injects its own `-O2` via `CFLAGS`/`CXXFLAGS`, and Meson appends environment flags *after* its own optimization flag on the compiler command line. GCC/Clang use the **last** `-O` flag, so conda-forge's `-O2` silently wins:
```
cc ... -O3 ... -march=nocona -mtune=haswell ... -O2 -ffunction-sections -pipe ... -c foo.c
```



This was first noticed via `sklearn/tree/meson.build`'s `override_options: ['optimization=3']` (an explicit ask that's supposed to matter for `_splitter.pyx`/`_partitioner.pyx`'s branch-heavy loops) silently doing nothing under conda-forge, but that's just the one place the override was visible enough to check.

This is a known Meson/conda-forge interaction, not new: mesonbuild/meson#15055 (closed as docs — "CFLAGS in general tend to override buildtype flags, as they are appended") and conda-forge/ctng-compiler-activation-feedstock#157 (still open/unmerged for gcc/Linux).

**However: benchmarking `-O2` vs `-O3` in isolation (real conda-forge toolchain) did not show any observable performance effect on what I tried for now.**. Contrary to an other conda-forge compilation chain setting that does cause an important slowdown on `ExtraTrees*`, see: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34869

For now, I'm not sure we should bother fixing it. Claude had a way to fix it, see PR #34864 (but I closed it for now).

title: [BUG] `compute_class_weight` coerces class labels to int in 1.9, breaking dict lookup for string labels
body: ### Introduce yourself hi, I am a core developer for the aeon toolkit and an academic at the university of Southampton. I found this bug when trying to raise our upper bound for scikit https://github.com/aeon-toolkit/aeon/pull/3787 For context, we have a range of algorithms that use scikit components, in this case the `ExtraTreeClassifier` and `RandomForestClassifier`. We also maintain a range of data archives including the UCR archive, hosted here http://timeseriesclassification.com/ Our classification data always loads class values as strings, so for example, "1"/"2" or "Run"/"Jump". The basic problem is that relevant parts of scikit 1.9 now always parse class value strings to integers, leading to dictionary errors. I had a good look and couldnt see this issue, sorry if its been fixed already. ### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact In 1.9, fitting a forest ensemble with `class_weight="balanced"` raises `ValueError` when the class labels are strings that happen to parse as integers ("1", "2", ...). The same code works in 1.8 and earlier. Labels that are genuine integers, or strings that do not parse as integers ("a", "b"), are unaffected. The problem comes from a coercion added to the user-defined-dictionary branch of compute_class_weight in #32644 (commit 9ca766b, "FEA Add array API support for LogisticRegression with LBFGS"): ```python for i, c in enumerate(classes): try: c = int(c) except ValueError: # `classes` contains strings c = str(c) if c in class_weight: ``` The intent looks like normalising array scalars to Python scalars so that dict lookup by key works under a non-numpy namespace. But int("1") succeeds, so it never reaches the except clause that would have preserved the string. That branch is reached even though the user asked for "balanced", because `BaseForest._validate_y_class_weight` does not pass "balanced" straight through. It round-trips (sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py:861): ```python # Computing class_weight (dict or list) for the "balanced" option. class_weight_k_vect = compute_class_weight("balanced", classes=self.classes_[k], ...) class_weight_k = {key: val for (key, val) in zip(self.classes_[k], class_weight_k_vect)} ... expanded_class_weight = compute_sample_weight(class_weight, y_original) ``` It first expands "balanced" into an explicit dict keyed by the original labels — {"1": 1.0, "2": 1.0}, string keys — and then feeds that dict back in. The second call goes through the dictionary branch, the keys are coerced to int, every lookup fails, and all classes are reported as unweighted. Estimators that pass "balanced" directly to `compute_class_weight (DecisionTreeClassifier, RidgeClassifierCV, SVC, ...)` take the dedicated `elif class_weight == "balanced"` branch, which uses a LabelEncoder and never coerces, so they are not affected. ### Steps/Code to Reproduce ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier X = np.random.RandomState(0).rand(20, 5) y = np.array(["1"] * 10 + ["2"] * 10) # string labels that parse as integers RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=5, class_weight="balanced").fit(X, y) ```` Or against compute_class_weight directly, without the forest: ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.utils.class_weight import compute_class_weight compute_class_weight( {"1": 1.0, "2": 1.0}, classes=np.array(["1", "2"]), y=np.array(["1", "2", "1"]) ) ``` ### Expected Results Expected Results Fits without error, as in 1.8.0 and earlier. The direct compute_class_weight call returns array([1., 1.]). ### Actual Results ```python-traceback Traceback (most recent call last): File "repro.py", line 7, in RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=5, class_weight="balanced").fit(X, y) File "sklearn/base.py", line 1403, in wrapper return fit_method(estimator, *args, **kwargs) File "sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py", line 393, in fit y, expanded_class_weight = self._validate_y_class_weight(y, sample_weight) File "sklearn/ensemble/_forest.py", line 879, in _validate_y_class_weight expanded_class_weight = compute_sample_weight(class_weight, y_original) File "sklearn/utils/_param_validation.py", line 191, in wrapper return func(*args, **kwargs) File "sklearn/utils/class_weight.py", line 236, in compute_sample_weight weight_k = compute_class_weight( File "sklearn/utils/_param_validation.py", line 191, in wrapper return func(*args, **kwargs) File "sklearn/utils/class_weight.py", line 117, in compute_class_weight raise ValueError( ValueError: The classes, [1, 2], are not in class_weight ``` The message is also misleading: it reports the classes as [1, 2] (post-coercion integers) when the real classes are the strings ["1", "2"], which are the dict keys. A mixed example shows the failure is per-label and driven purely by whether int() succeeds — with classes ["0", "a"] only "0" is reported: This effects both ExtraTreesClassifier and RandomForestClassifier ### Versions ```shell System: python: 3.12.9 [MSC v.1942 64 bit (AMD64)] machine: Windows-11-10.0.26200-SP0 Python dependencies: sklearn: 1.9.0 pip: 26.1.2 setuptools: 82.0.1 numpy: 2.4.6 scipy: 1.18.0 Cython: None pandas: 2.2.3 matplotlib: 3.10.1 joblib: 1.4.2 threadpoolctl: 3.5.0 ``` ### Interest in fixing the bug yes I would be happy to, I would not convert strings to ints at all, leave them as string and would not use a try ... except block in this context and avoid the round trip, but would need to look more closely, claude suggests this fix (and has helped me pin this down) ```python Convert the labels to Python scalars without altering their values, rather than parsing them. move_to is already imported and used earlier in the same function: for i, c in enumerate(classes): - try: - c = int(c) - except ValueError: # `classes` contains strings - c = str(c) + # convert to python scalars so that lookup by dict key works for any + # array namespace, without altering the label values themselves + for i, c in enumerate(move_to(classes, xp=np, device="cpu").tolist()): if c in class_weight: tolist() maps each element to its natural Python type — str stays str, int stays int — and both hash-match the user's dict keys, which is what the array-API port needed. Unlike int(), it never alters a label's value, so it cannot introduce this class of mismatch for any label type. ``` A narrower guard such as if not isinstance(c, str) around the existing int() call also fixes it, which is probably what I would do, but I obviously dont have the wider picture.

title: balanced_accuracy_score(adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the NaN filter

### Introduce yourself

I'm a data scientist in Toronto working on forecasting and causal inference. I've recently started contributing to scikit-learn — I have an open PR at #34888 (array API support for ShrunkCovariance) — and I found this while looking into #33712, where I was trying to work out which of two distinct undefined cases in balanced_accuracy_score that issue refers to. This one turned out to be independent of it, so I'm filing it separately.

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

balanced_accuracy_score(..., adjusted=True) returns -inf when a single class survives the internal NaN filter. The adjusted score is bounded — it spans [-1, 1], reaching -1 only at n_classes=2 — so -inf is outside the documented range of the metric.

This surfaces in cross-validation on small or imbalanced folds, where a fold can easily contain a single class. One -inf propagates through any mean over folds, turning the whole aggregate into -inf and silently destroying an otherwise valid CV score. The related nan case is at least absorbed by nan-aware aggregation; -inf is not.

Mechanism: n_classes is read after the NaN filter at _classification.py:2940, so when one class survives, chance = 1 / 1 and `score /= 1 - chance` at line 2946 divides by zero. The np.errstate guard wraps the per-class division only, not this one, and has been scoped that way since the original commit (e888c0d65cf, "ENH multiclass balanced accuracy" #10587, 2018) — the guard and the unguarded division were introduced together.

This is separate from #33712: it predates it and reproduces without touching replace_undefined_by.


### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
from sklearn.metrics import balanced_accuracy_score

# Case 1
print(balanced_accuracy_score([0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], adjusted=True))

# Case 2
print(balanced_accuracy_score([0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], adjusted=True))
```

## Expected Results

A value within the documented range of the adjusted metric, [-1, 1]. A score documented as bounded should not return -inf.

## Actual Results

On scikit-learn 1.9.0 (installed from PyPI), case 1 returns nan:

```
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:614: UserWarning: A single label was found in 'y_true' and 'y_pred'. For the confusion matrix to have the correct shape, use the 'labels' parameter to pass all known labels.
  warnings.warn(
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2946: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in scalar divide
  score /= 1 - chance
nan
```

Case 2 returns -inf:

```
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2939: UserWarning: y_pred contains classes not in y_true
  warnings.warn("y_pred contains classes not in y_true")
/tmp/sk19/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sklearn/metrics/_classification.py:2946: RuntimeWarning: divide by zero encountered in scalar divide
  score /= 1 - chance
-inf
```

Both RuntimeWarnings come from the same unguarded statement at line 2946. The texts differ — "invalid value" for case 1, "divide by zero" for case 2 — which maps onto the nan/-inf split: case 1 is 0/0, case 2 is -0.333/0.

Also reproduces unchanged on main (1.10.dev0), where the filter is at line 2969 and the division at line 2975.

title: [BUG] RidgeClassifierCV(scoring="accuracy", cv=None) returns incorrect best_score_ for binary classification
body:
### Introduce yourself

hello, I am a professor of computer science and a core developer at [aeon ](https://github.com/aeon-toolkit/aeon). We use RidgeClassifierCV as a classifier head for many of our transformation based pipelines and ensembles, particularly the convolution based ones, and this bug was found by our core dev Matthew (@MatthewMiddlehurst) when reviewing [this PR] (https://github.com/aeon-toolkit/aeon/pull/3655) that adapted one of these pipeline classifiers, the Arsenal, which is a component of our HIVE-COTEv2 classifier and is one of my finest moments in algorithm naming :)

### Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact

`RidgeClassifierCV(scoring="accuracy", cv=None)` computes an incorrect best_score_ for binary classification problems: it always returns accuracy of 1.0, even when the problem contains substantial label noise and the fitted classifier is clearly not perfect.

We use best_score_ as an estimate of each ensemble member's classification accuracy and use it as an ensemble weight. For multiclass problems this appears to work as expected. For binary problems, however, all ensemble members receive a weight of 1.0, effectively disabling the weighting mechanism.

The behaviour appears specific to the default cv=None path. Using an explicit cross-validation splitter such as cv=5 gives plausible accuracy scores.

Looking at the implementation, the cause may be the classification scoring code in the GCV path reconstructing class labels using `y.argmax(axis=1)`. For binary classification, LabelBinarizer produces a single-column target, so argmax(axis=1) is always zero.

### Steps/Code to Reproduce

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifierCV
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 20))
y = rng.randint(0, 2, size=200)

clf_loo = RidgeClassifierCV( alphas=[0.1, 1.0, 10.0], scoring="accuracy", ).fit(X, y)
clf_cv = RidgeClassifierCV( alphas=[0.1, 1.0, 10.0], scoring="accuracy", cv=5, ).fit(X, y)
print("cv=None best_score_:", clf_loo.best_score_)
print("cv=5 best_score_:", clf_cv.best_score_)
print("training accuracy:", clf_loo.score(X, y))

import sklearn;
sklearn.show_versions()
```
Outputs

cv=None best_score_: 1.0
cv=5 best_score_: 0.515
training accuracy: 0.65
```
on random data.

### Expected Results

an estimate of accuracy specific to the training data, not always 1.0.
